title: From Extractivism to Innovation Sovereignty : An Innovationological Framework for Critical Mineral Governance in the Democratic Republic of Congo
content: The accelerating global transition toward low-carbon energy systems has transformed critical minerals into strategic assets at the center of economic competitiveness, technological innovation, and geopolitical rivalry. As the world's leading producer of cobalt and one of the most mineral-endowed countries globally, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) occupies a pivotal position in emerging global value chains for electric mobility, renewable energy, battery technologies, and digital industries. Yet despite this extraordinary resource wealth, the country continues to experience persistent underdevelopment, institutional fragility, environmental degradation, and limited industrial transformation. Existing theoretical perspectives—including the resource curse, dependency theory, neo-extractivism, and global value chain analysis—provide important explanations for these outcomes but remain insufficient for conceptualizing pathways through which mineral abundance can be transformed into long-term innovation capacity and national prosperity. Building upon the emerging field of Innovationology, previously developed by Pitshou Moleka as a transdisciplinary science of innovation systems, adaptive intelligence, and societal transformation, this article proposes an Innovationological Framework for Critical Mineral Governance centered on the concept of innovation sovereignty. Innovation sovereignty is defined as the capacity of a nation to create, govern, retain, and continuously expand scientific, technological, industrial, institutional, and cognitive capabilities derived from its strategic resources. Rather than treating mining as an isolated extractive sector, the proposed framework conceptualizes critical minerals as catalysts for knowledge production, industrial learning, institutional adaptation, technological upgrading, and ecosystem-wide value creation. Drawing upon complexity science, systems thinking, innovation studies, adaptive governance, and sustainability transition scholarship, the article develops an integrated theoretical model explaining the transition from extractive dependence toward innovation-driven development. Although the Democratic Republic of Congo serves as the principal analytical case, the framework offers broader implications for mineral-rich economies seeking to reposition themselves within the rapidly evolving global green economy. The study contributes to innovation theory, natural resource governance, and African development by advancing innovation sovereignty as a new paradigm for governing critical minerals in the twenty-first century.
